stem.text: Yorkshire Brain Map School Workshop

lede.text:
Thank you for taking part in this workshop.

In this study, we'll use a special tool called electroencephalography (EEG) to collect information about your brain. We'll put sensors on your head, and they'll record your brain activity. A trained member of the research team will fit the headset and take the recording. The EEG headset should not feel uncomfortable, so if it does at any point, just let a member of the research team know. EEG is safe, pain free, and non-invasive.

In addition to EEG, we'll also ask questions about your life and how you feel. We made a list of questions that ask about things like who you are, how you feel, and how happy you are. We care about keeping your answers private. We'll ask for your name, date of birth and home address. We use them to keep your answers together if you take part again, to find your answers if you ask us to remove them, and — through a secure service called Connected West Yorkshire — to link your answers with your health and education records (we explain this on the consent screen). Your name, date of birth and address are kept apart from your answers. Only the research team and Connected West Yorkshire ever see them; researchers looking at the data only ever see a code.

Joining this study is your choice, and you can leave at any time with no problems. If you want to leave, please let a member of the research team or a teacher know.

Our study has permission from the School of Psychology Research Ethics Committee (Ethics Reference: SoPREC - 2026 4202-7027).

The questions take most people about 20 minutes. There's no rush: careful answers matter more than fast ones. Thank you for joining our study! If you have questions or worries, please ask a member of the research team.

moreInfo.label: How we look after your information

body.text:
WHAT WE COLLECT
Your answers to these questions, the EEG recording from the session, and some details about how you used the app — such as how long you spent on each question. We also collect your name, date of birth and home address, so the research team can identify your session, keep your answers together if you take part again, and link your answers with your health and education records (see below).

WHERE IT IS KEPT
Everything is saved on this iPad first, encrypted, so it works even with no internet. It is later transferred to secure University of Leeds storage. Your name, date of birth and address are stored apart from your answers, so they are not held together.

WHO CAN SEE IT
The research team. Connected West Yorkshire receives your name, date of birth and address, securely, only to link your records. When we publish or share the data, your name and address are never attached — only a study number and your answers.

YOUR ADDRESS
We ask for the address you live at most of the time. With your name and date of birth, it helps us keep your answers together if you take part more than once. It is never published. The only place it is sent is Connected West Yorkshire, securely, to link your records.

LINKING WITH OTHER RECORDS
Taking part includes this. Connected West Yorkshire uses your name, date of birth and address to join your answers to your health and education records, then takes them off and replaces them with a code before any researcher sees the data. You can ask us to stop at any time. The link continues for as long as the research goes on, and is used only for research.

CHANGING YOUR MIND
You can stop at any time, and you don't have to give a reason. If you want your answers taken out afterwards, contact Dr Sarmad Ali (S.A.Ali1@leeds.ac.uk) within one month of the workshop and tell him your name and date of birth.

QUESTIONS
Email Dr Sarmad Ali at S.A.Ali1@leeds.ac.uk. Ethics reference SoPREC - 2026 4202-7027.

lede.text:
Connected West Yorkshire is a secure research service that brings together information from the NHS, schools and councils in Yorkshire, so researchers can study what helps young people's health and learning.

Taking part in this study includes this: we will send your name, date of birth and address to Connected West Yorkshire. They use them only to find your health records (like GP and hospital visits) and education records (like attendance and exam results) and join them to your answers.

Before any researcher sees the joined-up information, your name, date of birth and address are taken off and replaced with a code. Researchers looking at it only ever see the code, so they cannot tell who you are from it. The one exception is safety: if you tell the research team something that makes them worried that you, or someone else, could be harmed, they will need to tell your school's safeguarding lead, as the statements below say.

The link continues for as long as the research goes on, including in future years, and is used only for research, unless you ask us to stop. You can stop it at any time by emailing Dr Sarmad Ali at S.A.Ali1@leeds.ac.uk, and you don't have to give a reason.

stem.text: Why your answers matter

lede.text:
There are no right or wrong answers – we are interested in your personal experiences.

What you tell us is used for research on how sleep, screens, and feelings fit together for people your age, and what we can do to help. That only works if the answers are really yours, including ones which may be less flattering.

A rushed or made-up answer causes the overall research picture to be slightly less true, affecting everyone the research is meant to help.

So take your time. And if you’d rather not answer something, you can leave it blank.

We want to note that some questions are about feelings, including difficult ones. You can skip any question or stop at any time. If anything upsets you, tell a member of the research team and they will make sure you're put in touch with someone at school who can help. Your answers are private: your teachers and family won't see them. The only exception is safety: if you tell us something that makes us worried that you, or someone else, could be harmed, we will need to tell your school's safeguarding lead so that you can get support.

ybm_hearing@1.0/en-GB/self/standard.name: YBM hearing (NHANES AUQ054, UK Biobank 2257)
ybm_hearing@1.0/en-GB/self/standard.construct: Self-rated hearing and difficulty hearing speech in background noise

provenance.basedOn: Two established self-report questions: NHANES (US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey) audiometry questionnaire item AUQ054, 'General condition of hearing' (e.g. 2015-2016 cycle, https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Nchs/Data/Nhanes/Public/2015/DataFiles/AUQ_I.htm), and UK Biobank touchscreen data-field 2257, 'Hearing difficulty with background noise'.
provenance.adaptations: Wording as given by the PI (November 2026). AUQ054: NHANES is interviewer-administered, with a proxy answering for under-16s; here pupils read and answer it themselves, and option 4 reads 'Moderate trouble' for NHANES's 'Moderate hearing trouble'. Field 2257: UK Biobank's answers are Yes / No / Do not know / Prefer not to answer; here 'Yes' is split into 'Yes, all or most of the time' and 'Yes, sometimes', and 'Prefer not to answer' is left out (any question can be skipped).
provenance.evidence: Single self-report items, widely used in adults (UK Biobank) and across ages (NHANES, by proxy under 16); not, as far as the record shows, validated as self-report in 11-18 year olds. Benchmarks: NHANES published distributions by age; UK Biobank (adults aged 40-69).
provenance.notes: Where the split of 'Yes' by frequency comes from is not recorded: to confirm with the PI.

provenance.basedOn: Pew Research Center, 2025 Teens Survey (Teens & Technology): US teens aged 13-17, n = 1,458, online, 25 September to 9 October 2025. Teen questions TCHATAWARE, TCHATUSE, TCHATFREQ, TCHATSPEC, TCHATWHY, TCHATFREQ2, TCHATHELPFUL, TCHATSCH1 and TCHATSCH2, as published in the toplines: 'How Teens Use and View AI', 24 February 2026, https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2026/02/PI_2026.02.24_Teens-and-AI_TOPLINE.pdf and 'Teens, Social Media and AI Chatbots 2025', 9 December 2025, https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2025/12/PI_2025.12.09_Teens-Social-Media-AI_TOPLINE.pdf.
provenance.adaptations: Wording and answer options are Pew's, word for word, apart from: each grid (TCHATSPEC, TCHATWHY, TCHATSCH1) is one screen per row, asked as a question ('Do you ever use ChatGPT?', 'Have you ever used AI chatbots to …?') with Pew's answer labels, in a fixed order where Pew randomises; Pew rotates some answer orders, here always shown in Pew's listed order; British spelling ('summarise', 'maths'). Added: Snapchat's My AI as a seventh chatbot, and two study-written questions (ai_felt_friend, ai_why_not_person). Each question's own record gives its Pew ID, Pew's wording and Pew's result.
provenance.evidence: Not a validated scale: single survey items from a national online survey of US teens. Benchmark: Pew's published results for US teens aged 13-17; compare this study's 13-17 year olds only, and allow for country, school setting (in class, on an iPad) and date.
provenance.notes: Chosen over study-written items so that answers can be compared with a published, regularly repeated source (PI's request, November 2026). UK figures to set alongside (no shared wording): Ofcom, Children and Parents: Media Use and Attitudes 2026 (56% of 8-17s have used AI); National Literacy Trust Annual Literacy Survey 2025 (66.5% of 13-18s use generative AI); Internet Matters, Me, Myself and AI, 2025 (64% of 9-17s use AI chatbots).
